title: Achievement Gaps Increase The Longer Kids Stay In School. Here’s Why.
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler challenges the widespread belief that income-based achievement gaps are driven by summer learning loss, and that longer school hours or year-round calendars are the fix. She notes that the classic Baltimore study is decades old and that more recent research finds gaps growing at roughly the same rate during the school year. Citing David Grissmer, she explains that a standard deviation represents far more learning in eighth grade than in first grade, so apparently stable gaps are actually widening, in line with the Matthew effect. Her conclusion is that America has a school problem, not a summer vacation problem, and that the place to look is what elementary schools teach. She argues that narrowed, test-prep driven curricula built around comprehension skills fail to build knowledge and vocabulary, hurting least-advantaged children most, so extra hours would only add more of a failed approach.
points: Recent evidence suggests gaps between rich and poor grow at about the same rate in school as over the summer, undermining the summer slide explanation.
Because a standard deviation in later grades equals many more grade levels of learning, a constant gap in standard deviations actually conceals widening gaps.
Gaps in reading are hardest to close later, so waiting to address them, as the Matthew effect predicts, makes them permanent.
Since high-stakes testing began in 2002, elementary curricula have narrowed to skills practice and test prep, crowding out the knowledge-building subjects.
Lengthening the school year without improving the knowledge content of the curriculum offers little benefit and may entrench the gaps.
quotes: One well-known study done in Baltimore found that nearly all of the gap between students at the top and bottom of the socioeconomic spectrum was due to “summer learning loss,” also known as “summer slide.” The researchers concluded that the gap was due to inequities in children’s lives outside of school, and that time in school was helping to compensate.

More recent research indicates that while most students lose some ground during the summer, especially in math, the gap between rich and poor doesn’t grow more then. It grows at pretty much the same rate as during the school year.

In the early grades, Grissmer said, a student only has to make up one grade level to move up a standard deviation. By eighth grade, moving up a standard deviation requires making up three grade levels. And in high school, the amount of learning that needs to be made up is so large that it may be impossible for students who are behind to catch up.
The longer you wait to address gaps in students’ reading ability, according to this theory, the wider the gaps get and the harder they are to narrow.

That widespread approach neither boosts test scores nor equips students with the knowledge and vocabulary they’ll need to understand what they’ll be expected to read in later years. And the students who suffer the most are the ones who are least likely to pick up academic knowledge and vocabulary outside school—those with less educated parents.
Since the advent of high-stakes reading and math tests in 2002, most elementary schools have narrowed the curriculum to spend more time on test prep.
Extending the school year would only make sense if we also improved the curriculum so that it focused on building students’ knowledge, beginning in kindergarten.
